Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Meridian Software pays its sales force either a 5% commission on gross revenue or a 10% commission on contribution margin (unit price $100 less $60 variable cost). On a typical order of 100 units at full list ($10,000 revenue), the revenue plan pays $500 versus $400 under the margin plan. Which statement best evaluates the two commission designs?

Choices.A: Contribution-margin commissions better align seller behavior with firm profitability because they discourage destructive discounting and steer selling effort toward the most profitable product mix.
Choices.B: Revenue commissions are strictly better - the higher payout motivates harder selling regardless of deal profitability.
Choices.C: The commission basis never affects how sellers price deals or which products they emphasize.
Choices.D: Margin-based commissions unlawfully reduce compensation the sales force has already earned.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: judging commission plans by payout size rather than by behavioral alignment with firm profit.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is A. Per IMA cost-management guidance, incentive plans should reward sellers on the outcome the firm values - contribution margin - not on gross revenue, which can be inflated by destructive discounting. On this order the margin plan pays ($100 - $60) x 100 units x 10% = $400 versus the revenue plan's $10,000 x 5% = $500. The margin plan pays slightly less yet automatically penalizes price concessions and favors high-margin mix, so seller behavior tracks firm profit. Business interpretation: a smaller average commission check can still be the superior design because it redirects effort toward profitable deals. Trap: equating a bigger commission payment with a better incentive system.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B mistakes payout size for incentive quality; a richer check on an unprofitable deal can destroy more margin than the extra effort adds, and the word strictly ignores how commission basis shifts discounting and product-mix behavior.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C assumes compensation design is behaviorally inert; commission basis demonstrably changes discounting discipline, product emphasis, and customer targeting, which is exactly why firms choose the margin base deliberately.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D misstates the law; commission structures are discretionary employer designs, and switching the measurement base to contribution margin alters only how variable pay accrues, not any earned-wage entitlement.
Topic: C.171 Commission basis and incentive alignment
VerifiedChecks: Independent: CM commissions penalize discounting and steer mix -> align

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Northgate Industries has regular capacity of 8,000 units at a $40 unit variable cost. A special order requests 9,000 units at $55 each; the final 1,000 units require overtime premium that lifts their variable cost to $48. Should Northgate accept, and what is the operating income effect?

Choices.A: Reject - the blended variable cost of about $40.89 leaves the $55 price looking thin.
Choices.B: Accept - operating income rises $127,000 (the first 8,000 units earn a $15 margin each and the final 1,000 earn $7 each).
Choices.C: Accept - income rises $165,000 by treating every unit at the regular variable cost.
Choices.D: Accept - income rises $63,000 by treating every unit at the overtime cost.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: averaging variable costs across capacity tiers instead of analyzing each tier separately.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is B. Under relevant-costing rules in the IMA Decision Analysis domain, each unit must carry the cost tier that actually produces it. Incremental revenue = 9,000 x $55 = $495,000. Incremental variable cost = (8,000 x $40) + (1,000 x $48) = $320,000 + $48,000 = $368,000. Net operating income effect = $495,000 - $368,000 = +$127,000, so Northgate should accept. Unit margins are $15 on regular-capacity units and $7 on overtime units; both tiers exceed zero, so no tier destroys value. Business interpretation: a discounted special order is worthwhile when every production tier covers its own incremental cost. Trap: blending the $40 and $48 tiers into one average rate obscures the fact that both remain profitable and can trigger an unjustified rejection.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A averages regular and overtime cost into one blended figure and compares it with price; tier-by-tier analysis shows each tier contributes positively ($15 then $7 per unit), so rejecting forfeits $127,000 of real income.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C applies the regular $40 cost to all 9,000 units and skips the overtime tier; the $8-per-unit premium on the final 1,000 units is a genuine incremental cost, so the claimed figure overstates income by ignoring it.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D charges the $48 overtime cost against all 9,000 units, shrinking every unit margin to $7; the premium applies only to the final 1,000 units, so the actual gain of $127,000 is about double the stated $63,000.
Topic: C.172 Special order straddling overtime tiers
VerifiedChecks: Independent: 368K total VC vs 495K revenue -> +127K accept

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Crestline Division reports an operating loss after absorbing $500,000 of headquarters cost allocations. Before those unavoidable allocations, the division's contribution is positive $200,000. What should management do?

Choices.A: Drop the division - a reported loss always demands immediate corrective action.
Choices.B: Keep the division but force it to absorb a larger allocation share until it breaks even.
Choices.C: Keep the division - it covers its own traceable costs and contributes $200,000 toward unavoidable headquarters costs that continue anyway, so closing it would cut company income by $200,000.
Choices.D: Drop the division only if a reported loss persists beyond two consecutive years.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: treating unavoidable allocated headquarters costs as avoidable in a keep-or-drop decision.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is C. Keep-or-drop analysis counts only the costs that actually disappear if the segment closes. The $500,000 headquarters allocation is unavoidable and continues regardless, while Crestline earns +$200,000 above its own traceable costs. Dropping the division forfeits that $200,000 contribution yet eliminates none of the allocated cost, so consolidated income falls by $200,000. Per IMA decision-analysis guidance, allocated common costs are irrelevant to the drop decision. Business interpretation: GAAP-style allocations can dress a healthy contributor as a loser, and acting on the dressed-up number destroys real income. Trap: treating allocated headquarters costs as avoidable in a keep-or-drop decision.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A reacts to the allocation-inflated reported loss instead of the segment's own economics; traceable revenues exceed traceable costs by $200,000, so the reported loss is an accounting artifact rather than an operating verdict.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B manipulates an arbitrary allocation formula instead of economics; reshuffling overhead among segments redraws internal reports without changing the $200,000 of real contribution the division delivers.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D swaps analysis for a calendar rule; how long an allocation-driven loss has persisted says nothing about whether the segment's traceable contribution is positive today.
Topic: C.173 GAAP allocations masking a contributor

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Ardent Manufacturing estimates demand of 12,000 units with probability 0.30, 9,000 units with probability 0.50, and 6,000 units with probability 0.20. Plant capacity is 9,000 units and contribution margin is $10 per unit sold. What expected contribution should Ardent plan on?

Choices.A: $93,000 - weighting raw demand with no regard for capacity.
Choices.D: $84,000 - strong-demand sales truncate at the 9,000-unit capacity cap.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: failing to truncate demand scenarios at available capacity before computing an expectation.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is D. Expected sales must respect physical capacity: the 12,000-unit demand scenario can sell only 9,000. Expected unit sales = (0.30 x 9,000) + (0.50 x 9,000) + (0.20 x 6,000) = 2,700 + 4,500 + 1,200 = 8,400 units. Expected contribution = 8,400 x $10 = $84,000. Uncapped weighting would give 9,300 units and $93,000, overstating the plan by $9,000. Per expected-value technique in the IMA Decision Analysis coverage, probabilities weight feasible outcomes only. Business interpretation: budgeting beyond capacity writes shortages into the master budget and misstates planned contribution. Trap: failing to truncate demand scenarios at available capacity before computing an expectation.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A weights untruncated demand (0.30 x 12,000 + 0.50 x 9,000 + 0.20 x 6,000 = 9,300 units); the strong-demand scenario cannot sell past the 9,000-unit cap, so 900 phantom units inflate the result by $9,000.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B matches no supported calculation; it equals neither the capped expectation ($84,000), the uncapped one ($93,000), nor any single scenario's contribution.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C anchors on the weakest scenario (6,000 units x $10); expected value weights all scenarios by probability rather than planning around the worst case.
VerifiedChecks: Independent: sales EV capped: 8,400 units x $10 = $84,000

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: A critical parts shortage has halted Kestrel Fabricators' production line, forfeiting $18,000 of contribution per day. Expediting replacement parts carries a $6,000 freight premium and shortens the outage by 2 days. What should Kestrel do?

Choices.A: Expedite - avoiding 2 days of lost contribution ($36,000) outweighs the $6,000 premium by $30,000.
Choices.B: Wait - freight premiums are pure waste with no measurable offset.
Choices.C: Expedite - premium freight always pays for itself.
Choices.D: Wait - 2 days falls inside the standard safety window.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: rejecting expedited freight as waste without netting it against quantified avoided downtime losses.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is A. Compare relevant benefit with relevant cost: expediting preserves 2 days x $18,000/day = $36,000 of contribution and costs a $6,000 premium, a net advantage of $36,000 - $6,000 = +$30,000. Per relevant-costing principles in the IMA Decision Analysis domain, the decision rests on future differential amounts - the premium is differential and the preserved contribution is genuinely forgone income. Business interpretation: downtime cost, not the freight quote, sets the urgency standard for spare-parts logistics. Trap: reflexively labeling expedited freight as waste without netting it against quantified avoided losses.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B declares the premium waste without netting it against avoided downtime; the $6,000 outlay purchases $36,000 of preserved contribution, a six-fold return on the spend.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C lands on the right action through a false absolute; expediting wins here only because measured downtime loss dwarfs the premium, and different numbers could flip the conclusion.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D leans on an unquantified policy window; safety-stock rules govern inventory buffers, but a stopped line bleeding $18,000 of contribution per day is the operative clock, and it argues for speed.
Topic: C.175 Expedited freight versus downtime contribution

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Vertex Analytics prices verified education accounts 60% below its commercial tier, and commercial customers are objecting. VP of Pricing Angela Ruiz, with controller sign-off, reviews the record: education-segment demand is far more elastic, marginal delivery cost is near zero, eligibility gating is independently verified, and no resale leakage has been detected. What should Ruiz recommend?

Choices.A: Move to uniform global pricing - differentiated pricing is indefensible whenever any customer complains.
Choices.B: Maintain differentiated EDU pricing with verified gating plus quarterly leakage monitoring - the willingness-to-pay differences are large, verifiable, and non-leaking, the conditions legitimate price discrimination requires.
Choices.C: Eliminate the paid commercial tier and migrate every customer to EDU pricing.
Choices.D: Match whatever coupon a competitor issues in any segment, without verification.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: dismantling a defensible price structure under pressure from high-willingness-pay complainants.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is B. Price discrimination withstands scrutiny when (1) elasticity differences are genuine and material, (2) segmentation is enforceable at low cost, and (3) resale leakage stays contained. All three hold here: independently verified EDU gating, near-zero marginal delivery cost, and zero observed leakage. Keeping the structure preserves fat contribution margins from low-elasticity commercial users while expanding volume among high-elasticity education users, consistent with IMA pricing guidance that price should track delivered value, not cost alone. Quarterly leakage monitoring keeps condition (3) testable as markets evolve, and controller sign-off documents the review. Trap: abandoning a sound segmentation architecture because its beneficiaries under uniform pricing complain loudest.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A lets complaint pressure override economic evidence; uniform pricing would surrender substantial contribution from price-sensitive education users while winning commercial customers who were never going to leave.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C dismantles the price architecture; moving high-willingness commercial users onto EDU rates donates the segmentation margin that funds product investment and invites capacity strain.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D outsources pricing strategy to rival promotions and drops verification entirely; unverified matching invites resale arbitrage and teaches customers to await coupons, corroding both segments.
VerifiedChecks: Independent: verified non-leaking segment pricing sustains

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Calderon Precision runs a constrained line 2,000 hours per year; each unit takes 1 hour of constraint time and earns $25 of contribution if it passes inspection. First-pass yield is 92%. A $1,800 training program would raise first-pass yield to 97%. What net annual benefit should Calderon expect from the training?

Choices.A: $2,500 - the gross improvement in annual throughput value.
Choices.C: Net +$700 per year - $2,500 of added contribution less the $1,800 training cost.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: quoting gross constraint improvement without netting the cost of the intervention that produces it.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is C. Value on a constrained resource flows from good output per bottleneck hour. Today: 0.92 x $25 = $23.00 of contribution per hour. After training: 0.97 x $25 = $24.25 per hour. Annual gain = $1.25 x 2,000 hours = $2,500. Net of the $1,800 program, year-one benefit = $2,500 - $1,800 = +$700, so the project proceeds. Per theory-of-constraints logic in the IMA Decision Analysis coverage, quality improvements AT the constraint convert directly into saleable throughput. Business interpretation: a five-point yield gain is worth $2,500 a year only because it lands on the bottleneck. Trap: quoting gross improvement and forgetting the cost of the intervention that produces it.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A stops at the gross throughput gain (($24.25 - $23.00) x 2,000 hours = $2,500) and omits the $1,800 training outlay; decisions net benefits against the cost of obtaining them.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B invents a half-year horizon found nowhere in the facts; the yield uplift and the training invoice both land in the same full year, yielding $2,500 - $1,800 = $700.
ExplanationWrongD: Option D cannot be rebuilt from the given data; it scales the five-point yield gain incorrectly and misses that each constraint hour produces one full unit whose pass rate drives the entire $25 contribution.
Topic: C.177 Value of a yield improvement on the constraint

Authorities: IMA CMA Part 2 Content Specification Outline (Decision Analysis)
Stem: Halbrook Distribution is evaluating closure of its leased warehouse. Closing saves $120,000 of lease, $80,000 of staff, and $30,000 of utilities annually, but triggers a one-time $45,000 termination penalty plus $35,000 of stock-transfer handling and adds $60,000 per year of transportation cost to serve customers from the main site. What is the year-one financial effect of closing?

Choices.D: +$90,000 net in year one, improving thereafter as the one-time costs fall away.

CommonTrapReference: Trap: omitting newly created recurring costs when evaluating facility closures.
ExplanationCorrect: The correct answer is D. Year-one relevant analysis: avoidable recurring savings = $120,000 + $80,000 + $30,000 = $230,000. Year-one closure costs = $45,000 termination penalty + $35,000 transfer handling + $60,000 incremental transportation = $140,000. Net year-one effect = $230,000 - $140,000 = +$90,000. From year two onward only the recurring $60,000 transportation burden remains, lifting the annual net benefit to +$170,000. Per IMA relevant-costing standards, one-time exit costs are relevant in the year incurred but do not recur. Business interpretation: closure is modestly positive in year one and clearly positive thereafter. Trap: dropping the newly created recurring transport cost or mishandling one-time items.
ExplanationWrongA: Option A totals the three recurring savings and stops; it ignores the $45,000 penalty, the $35,000 handling charge, and the $60,000 transport increase that together trim the year-one benefit to $90,000.
ExplanationWrongB: Option B nets the one-time items but drops the ongoing $60,000 transportation increase; that cost recurs every year, converting the claimed $150,000 into a $90,000 year-one net.
ExplanationWrongC: Option C flips signs in the arithmetic; savings enter positively ($230,000) while the $80,000 of combined one-time costs and the $60,000 transport increase subtract, leaving a positive $90,000 rather than a loss.
